nodes.label: The block-character wordmark
nodes.rationale: Twelve rows of sixty block-drawing characters in the yellow the window tabs use. As text it is crisp at any size, weighs nothing, scales with the viewport and can be selected - all of which a PNG gives up. line-height: 1 and no letter-spacing are what make the blocks meet.

nodes.label: get-and-run-kosmos.sh - one command to run it
nodes.rationale: Nothing to clone, nothing to build, no toolchain. It fetches the newest published image, the runner and a disk; QEMU is the only thing it cannot fetch. The framebuffer size is compiled in, so a different resolution is a different image.

nodes.label: Two QEMU flags that are not guessable
nodes.rationale: virtio-mmio.force-legacy=false, because QEMU's virtio-mmio devices default to the legacy interface which this driver correctly refuses - without it there is no keyboard and no pointer and it looks like a Kosmos bug. And virtio-tablet-device rather than a mouse: a tablet reports absolute position, so the guest cursor cannot drift away from the real one.

nodes.label: Only macOS is tested
nodes.rationale: Linux and Windows should both work - nothing in the image knows what host it is on - but they have not been run, and saying otherwise would be pretending.

nodes.label: What it is not: Unix, Windows, macOS, AmigaOS, a BeOS clone
nodes.rationale: No fork, exec, signals, pipes, sockets, select, ioctl, file descriptors, or a path reachable without a namespace. AmigaOS's lack of memory protection is the thing this is furthest from. And not a BeOS clone though BeOS is the reference: BeOS was monolithic, and the architecture underneath here is QNX's.

nodes.label: C and Lua, and nothing else
nodes.source_location: What it is trying to be
nodes.rationale: C for the kernel, drivers, servers and pixel loops - a small language that compiles to what you expect, which is the whole requirement for parts that run on behalf of someone else. Lua for applications: a syntax you can hold in your head and no compiler.

nodes.label: A blank canvas you can write applications on, without a toolchain
nodes.source_location: What it is trying to be
nodes.rationale: An application here is a text file in /bin and the machine can write and run one without a rebuild. Most operating systems ask you to install gigabytes of compilers before you can make the machine do something new; this one asks you to open the editor.

nodes.label: The C/Lua line is a layer, not a judgement
nodes.rationale: It used to be a judgement call about which servers were on a hot path, and the audio server was written in Lua because nobody recognised that a period is a frame with a different clock. It spun, it allocated inside a 5.8 ms deadline, and it could not print a diagnostic.

nodes.rationale: An index into your own table, never a global identifier. What you were not given, you cannot name.

nodes.label: The desktop, from BeOS
nodes.rationale: The yellow tab only as wide as its title rather than a bar across the window; the Deskbar in the corner; replicants; typed attributes with live queries; responsiveness as a design constraint rather than an optimisation.

nodes.label: A live image, from Lisp Machines
nodes.source_location: And the rest of what it is built out of
nodes.rationale: The system can write and run its own programs, and you can script a running application from the shell without it having any scripting code in it.

nodes.label: Control by message, data by shared memory
nodes.rationale: The language's data model where the shape is the caller's to choose, a declared struct where the shape is agreed. Two reasons found by building it rather than planning it: a server has to stay correct when its caller is wrong, and a garbage collector cannot sit where something else's timing depends on it.

nodes.label: The audio server taught the rule
nodes.rationale: It took a 1024-byte period as a message payload 172 times a second, meaning a Lua string allocated on each side of every one: 340 KB a second of garbage inside a 5.8 ms deadline. It played, and it jittered, and no amount of scheduling fixed it - the collector was in the audio path by construction.

nodes.label: 0.9 - a second architecture
nodes.rationale: x86-64 as well as AArch64, running the whole desktop. All thirteen kernel/ files compile for both with no #ifdef, and the display harness passes the same sixty-two checks on each board in the same time.

nodes.label: 0.8 - a web browser, and a network under it
nodes.rationale: NetSurf's hubbub, libdom and libcss vendored unpatched on a freestanding libc. TCP so a page can come off the real internet, and an HTTP server to go the other way. The allocator learned to grow. And the 64-bit-only line was drawn deliberately, which is what ruled the Pi 1 out.

nodes.label: 0.7 - the servers moved to C, one at a time
nodes.rationale: Audio first because it sits on a deadline and proved the point; then the small ones, then the filesystem and the console. Hot reload was removed rather than argued for, having run out of things to reload.

nodes.label: 0.6 - the desktop
nodes.rationale: A window manager, a widget kit, a Deskbar, and applications that are separate processes talking by message.

nodes.label: See it running - the screenshots
nodes.rationale: desktop.png, cern.png, demos.png, network.png, browser.png. All software rendered - there is no GPU driver; the compositor blits at about 6.5 ns a pixel, six TinyGL demos run at 41 fps and glxgears at 61.

nodes.label: What there is to try
nodes.rationale: wm browser, wm tracker, wm terminal, wm cube3d, wm doom, wm paint, ping 8.8.8.8, wm webserver.

nodes.label: Versions are major.minor.revision
nodes.rationale: A revision per push, a minor when something substantial lands. There is no release schedule and nothing is stable - the version number is a bookmark, not a promise.
